whyThisMatters: In the first minute of a real incident, most people freeze or try to fix it alone. The habit that helps you is knowing your next step before you need it.
rememberThis: STOP, VERIFY, REPORT. Use this order every time, no matter what the situation looks like.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group what they would do in the first few seconds of each scenario. Ask before you show the good answer.
For the phone-call case, ask if anyone has a trusted number they know by heart to call back on — or would they need to look it up under pressure?
Ask why "wait and see if anything goes wrong" feels tempting, even though it is the wrong choice in every case here.
Ask how it felt to decide under time pressure. Was it harder to pause when the clock was running?
For the video-call case, ask if anyone would feel okay ending a call with a senior leader to go and check.
Ask the group to name their own trusted way to check an urgent request. Do this for each role here: Finance, HR, Operations, and Offshore.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is trying to fix it yourself before reporting. People change their own password, restart a locked computer, or move a leaked folder. It feels helpful, but it often destroys evidence that the IT support team needs. People also most often get the video-call case wrong, choosing "approve the payment" because the face and voice matched — a live call feels harder to fake than an email.

cases.title: You Clicked a Link in a Seafarer Follow-Up
cases.scenario: You work in Crewing. You are checking emails from seafarers and manning agents. You click a link in what looked like a normal follow-up — "Re: Application — 2nd Engineer, MV Horizon". After you click, the page looks wrong and a login box pops up.

decisions.prompt: The page that opened looks strange. It asks you to log in again. What do you do first?

options.text: Type your work password to see if it is real
options.feedback: Do not type your password on a strange page. Even a quick test can give away your login to attackers.

options.text: Close the tab without typing anything and leave the device alone
options.feedback: Right choice. Not typing anything stops the attack. Leaving the device as it is keeps what the IT support team needs to see.

options.text: Take a screenshot to show a crewing colleague before you do anything else
options.feedback: Sharing it with colleagues first slows you down. The most important step is to tell the IT support team fast, not to ask others first.

cases.debrief: Whether it is a link, an attachment, or anything unexpected, the steps are the same. STOP before you do more. Do not touch the device more than you need to. REPORT right away with details. Every minute you wait is a minute the IT support team does not have.

cases.title: The Payroll Details Text
cases.scenario: You get a text that looks like it is from HR Payroll: "Synergy HR — click here to update your bank details for this month's allotment. Action needed today or your pay will be delayed." It includes a link you have never seen before.

options.text: Tap the link and update your details quickly so your pay is not delayed
options.feedback: Tapping an unknown link to "update" bank details is exactly how these texts steal your login — no real payroll deadline is worth that risk.

options.text: Do not tap the link — open the official crew/HR portal from your bookmark and report the text to the IT support team
options.feedback: Right call. Going straight to a place you already trust removes the attacker's link completely, and reporting it helps flag the pattern for others.

options.text: Reply to the text asking if it is really from HR
options.feedback: Replying only confirms your number is active — it does not prove anything, because a fake text will simply say yes.

cases.debrief: STOP — do not tap the link. VERIFY by opening the official HR or crew portal yourself (from a bookmark you already have) or by calling HR on a number you already know. REPORT the text to the IT support team.

cases.title: You Found an Unknown USB Stick
cases.scenario: You are on board MV Horizon and you find a small USB stick — a thumb drive — taped to a shared computer on the bridge. It has no label and no clear owner.

decisions.prompt: No one says it is theirs and you are curious. What do you do?

options.text: Plug it into the shared computer to check what is on it
options.feedback: An unknown stick can install harmful software the moment you plug it in. Plugging it in just to look is how it gets in.

options.text: Leave it unplugged and tell the IT support team — do not try to find the owner yourself
options.feedback: Correct. Not plugging it in removes the risk. It is not your job to find out who owns it — let the IT support team handle it safely.

options.text: Ask around the crew mess if anyone is missing a USB stick
options.feedback: This feels helpful, but it wastes time. Word can also reach the person who left it there before the IT support team sees it.

cases.debrief: An unknown USB stick is an easy way for harmful software to get into a system. STOP before you plug anything in. REPORT it directly to the IT support team so it is checked properly — do not leave it in a drawer or pass it around.

cases.title: The Video Call From a Senior Leader
cases.scenario: You are on a video call with someone who looks and sounds exactly like a senior finance leader. Their picture freezes for a second and the lighting looks a little off, but they speak with full confidence. They ask you to approve an unusual vendor payment — USD 48,500 for provisions — right now, before the call ends.

options.text: Approve the payment — the face and voice matched, so it must really be them
options.feedback: A real-looking face and voice on a call is not proof of who someone is. Both can now be faked. An unusual, urgent payment is exactly when to STOP and VERIFY using a number or channel you already had before this call. Then REPORT anything strange.

options.text: Quietly stall by saying you will do it after the call, hoping they forget
options.feedback: A real-looking face and voice on a call is not proof of who someone is. Both can now be faked. An unusual, urgent payment is exactly when to STOP and VERIFY using a number or channel you already had before this call. Then REPORT anything strange.

options.text: End the call and check the request by contacting that leader on a number or channel you already know is real
options.feedback: Correct. A real-looking face and voice is not proof. An unusual, urgent payment is exactly when to STOP and VERIFY using a number or channel you already had before this call. Then REPORT anything strange.

options.text: Ask a colleague in chat if they got the same request, then decide
options.feedback: A real-looking face and voice on a call is not proof of who someone is. Both can now be faked. An unusual, urgent payment is exactly when to STOP and VERIFY using a number or channel you already had before this call. Then REPORT anything strange.

cases.debrief: A convincing face and voice is not proof of identity — treat an unusual, urgent request the same on video as you would over email: STOP, VERIFY through a number or channel you already had before this call, then REPORT.

cases.title: Your Work Laptop Went Missing
cases.scenario: You just finished a vessel visit at the port. You travelled back on the launch, and when you get to the jetty you realise your work laptop is gone — it was in your bag during the transfer.

decisions.prompt: You just noticed it is gone. What do you do first?

options.text: Go back to the jetty and the launch to search for it yourself
options.feedback: Every minute you spend searching is a minute the IT support team is not locking your accounts or wiping the device. Speed matters more than searching.

options.text: Report it to the IT support team and your manager immediately
options.feedback: Correct. Fast reporting lets the IT support team act while there is still time to lock things.

cases.debrief: A missing device with company access is a race against time. STOP trying to find it yourself. REPORT right away to the IT support team and your manager with what you know. Check that the next steps happened, like locking the device remotely and changing your password.

cases.title: The Seafarer CV Attachment
cases.scenario: A message looks like it is from your usual crewing portal. It forwards a seafarer CV as an attachment — "2nd Engineer, MV Horizon — available immediately." But the sender address is spelled a little differently than normal (a missing letter or added word). It says the candidate needs an answer "within the hour" or they will take another offer.

options.text: Open the attachment quickly so you do not lose a strong candidate
options.feedback: A small spelling change in the sender address plus fake urgency is a classic trap. Attackers know Crewing often gets CVs from strangers. STOP, VERIFY, and REPORT applies to a seafarer file just like any other email.

options.text: Reply to the sender asking for more information
options.feedback: A small spelling change in the sender address plus fake urgency is a classic trap. Attackers know Crewing often gets CVs from strangers. STOP, VERIFY, and REPORT applies to a seafarer file just like any other email.

options.text: STOP before opening anything, VERIFY the sender's exact email address and the crewing portal directly, then REPORT if it does not check out
options.feedback: A small spelling change in the sender address plus fake urgency is a classic trap. Attackers know Crewing often gets CVs from strangers. STOP, VERIFY, and REPORT applies to a seafarer file just like any other email.

options.text: Forward it to a crewing colleague and let them decide
options.feedback: A small spelling change in the sender address plus fake urgency is a classic trap. Attackers know Crewing often gets CVs from strangers. STOP, VERIFY, and REPORT applies to a seafarer file just like any other email.

cases.debrief: A misspelled sender address plus made-up urgency is a classic lure — the Crewing inbox gets CVs from strangers every day, so STOP, VERIFY, REPORT applies here just like anywhere else.

cases.title: You Suspect a Data Leak
cases.scenario: You are in the shared drive and notice that crew allotment and payroll files — which should only be visible to HR and Finance — are now in a folder anyone in the company can open.

decisions.prompt: You just spotted this. What do you do first?

options.text: Message a few colleagues to see if they have noticed it too
options.feedback: Telling others, even inside the company, can spread sensitive details before the IT support team has checked what happened.

options.text: Do not tell colleagues widely and do not touch the files — report it to the IT support team right away
options.feedback: Correct. Not talking about it widely and not touching the files keeps the evidence safe for the IT support team.

cases.debrief: A possible data leak is like a scene you should not touch. STOP before you talk about it more widely or try to fix it yourself. Note what you saw without changing anything. REPORT right away so the trained team can take over.

cases.title: Skip the Permit Sign-Off?
cases.scenario: You get a Teams message — Teams is the work chat app — from someone you do not recognise. No photo, no chat history. They say the site supervisor cannot be reached. They ask you to skip the permit-to-work sign-off — the signed safety approval before hot work or enclosed-space entry — "just this once" so the schedule does not slip.

decisions.prompt: What is the warning sign here?

options.text: It is fine — schedules matter, and you can sort out the paperwork later
options.feedback: An unknown sender, time pressure, and a request to skip a safety check are the warning signs. Skipping a required safety approval because an urgent, unreachable person said so is the red flag — the same trick as a fake-boss email asking for a wire transfer, just aimed at a safety step instead of money.

options.text: Someone you cannot verify is pressuring you to skip a safety approval, using urgency and "the boss is unreachable" as the excuse
options.feedback: Correct. An unknown sender, time pressure, and a request to skip a safety check are the warning signs. Skipping a required safety approval because an urgent, unreachable person said so is the red flag — the same trick as a fake-boss email asking for a wire transfer, just aimed at a safety step instead of money.

options.text: It is a normal, routine reminder about the schedule
options.feedback: An unknown sender, time pressure, and a request to skip a safety check are the warning signs. Skipping a required safety approval because an urgent, unreachable person said so is the red flag — the same trick as a fake-boss email asking for a wire transfer, just aimed at a safety step instead of money.

options.text: It is expected — supervisors often message from other accounts
options.feedback: An unknown sender, time pressure, and a request to skip a safety check are the warning signs. Skipping a required safety approval because an urgent, unreachable person said so is the red flag — the same trick as a fake-boss email asking for a wire transfer, just aimed at a safety step instead of money.

cases.debrief: An unverified sender plus time pressure plus a request to skip a normal check is the same pattern as a fake-boss scam — just aimed at a safety process instead of a payment.

cases.title: You Got a Suspicious Phone Call on Board
cases.scenario: The ship's phone rings on the bridge. Someone says they are from head-office IT support. They say there is a problem with your crew portal account and ask you to confirm your password and a code from your phone right now.

decisions.prompt: The caller wants you to say your password and a code right now. What do you do?

options.text: Give a partial answer to seem cooperative without giving everything
options.feedback: Even a small hint can be enough. The caller only needs one true detail to build the rest.

options.text: Do not give out any passwords, codes, or personal details — offer to call back on a trusted number instead
options.feedback: Correct. The real IT support team will never ask you to say your password on a call they made to you.

cases.debrief: Urgency on a call is a trick, not a real deadline. STOP before you share anything. Hang up and call back on a number you already trust — for example, the IT helpdesk number in the crew portal or your handbook. REPORT the attempt so others can be warned.

cases.title: Your Screen Just Locked
cases.scenario: A message covers your office computer screen. It says your files are locked and you must pay to get them back. A countdown timer is running. This is ransomware — harmful software that locks your files until you pay.

options.text: Try to pay quickly before the timer runs out
options.feedback: Paying does not guarantee you get your files back. It also funds the next attack. And you skip reporting, which is what the IT support team needs most.

options.text: Disconnect the computer from the network right away (unplug the cable or turn off Wi-Fi) and leave it alone
options.feedback: Right idea. Disconnecting quickly can stop it from spreading to other computers before the IT support team steps in.

options.text: Post about it in the team chat to warn others
options.feedback: This is understandable, but it is not the fastest way to contain it. It can also cause panic before the IT support team knows how far it has spread.

cases.debrief: Ransomware — harmful software that locks your files for payment — wants you to panic and pay. STOP by disconnecting the computer from the network right away (unplug the cable or turn off Wi-Fi). Do not try to pay or fix it yourself. REPORT fast to the IT support team so they can stop it from reaching other systems.
